title: As one housing reform works in Texas, another in Colorado hits a budgetary hitch
gist: A paywalled teaser reporting that Texas House Bill 24, passed the prior year, is already changing housing outcomes on the ground by neutralizing a Jim Crow-era state law, while a parallel Colorado housing reform runs into a budget problem.

insights.claim: Texas House Bill 24, passed the prior year, is already proving effective at changing housing outcomes on the ground, according to the Texas Tribune.
insights.speaker: Halina Bennet
insights.so_what: Early evidence that a state-level zoning/land-use reform actually moves construction is a signal for housing-supply-linked markets and for other states considering copycat bills.
insights.quote: House Bill 24 took the wind out of the sails of a Jim Crow-era state law
insights.locator: A bill Texas passed last year

insights.claim: Texas House Bill 24 curtailed a Jim Crow-era state law that had let neighboring property owners obstruct nearby development.
insights.speaker: Halina Bennet
insights.so_what: Removing neighbor-veto mechanisms is the concrete lever through which supply reform translates into more building; watch for similar veto-stripping provisions elsewhere.
insights.locator: A bill Texas passed last year

insights.claim: A Colorado housing reform has run into a budgetary hitch, raising the question of what happens to the push for more housing when the budget dries up.
insights.speaker: Halina Bennet
insights.so_what: Reforms that depend on state spending are more fragile than pure deregulatory ones when fiscal conditions tighten — a distinction worth tracking across state housing agendas.
insights.quote: What happens to the push for more housing when the budget dries up?
